# Preface {.unnumbered}

You already own the best astronomy lab there is. It is over your head every
clear night, it costs nothing, and the Moon is in it most evenings. This book
is short on purpose, so you spend less time reading about the sky and more
time looking at it.

Every chapter follows one lecture. Read it before class, or after, or the
night before the exam. I will not judge. (I will, a little.)

## What this book is

Two courses, four lectures each, eight chapters.

- **AST 101, The Night Sky**: the celestial sphere and daily motion, the
  phases of the Moon and eclipses, the seasons, and light and telescopes.
- **AST 102, Stars and Galaxies**: measuring the stars, the lives of stars,
  galaxies and dark matter, and the expanding universe.

No physics background is assumed. The math is ratios, angles and the
occasional division. A calculator is welcome; fear is not required.

## How to use it

**Predict first.** Each chapter asks you questions before it answers them.
Stop and commit to an answer, even a wild one. A wrong prediction you have
written down teaches you more than a right answer you only read.

**Draw everything.** Most of AST 101 comes down to a few pictures: the Sun,
Earth and Moon seen from above, and your horizon seen from the ground. If you
can draw them from memory, you can work out the rest.

**Check yourself.** Every chapter ends with a self-check. Click an answer to
see whether you were right and why. The self-checks are not graded.

**Go outside.** Each chapter has something to look for in the real sky. Do
it, and put it in your observing log.

## Where this fits

The book sits next to two other things you will use all term:

- **The lecture slides**, one deck per lecture, with the same titles as the
  sections here.
- **Astra**, the course's AI tutor. Astra knows these chapters, the slides
  and the problem sets, and it teaches the way I do: it will ask you to
  predict, hand you hints, and refuse to do your homework. Each learning goal
  on Astra's map links to the section of this book that teaches it.

If something here disagrees with the slides, or with Astra, tell me. One of
us is wrong, and finding out which is a perfectly good use of office hours.

*Dr. Alex Morgan*
